articles.headline: SOMEWHAT DISFIGURED
articles.text:
SOMEWHAT DISFIGURED

But Still in the Ring—He Laughs Best Who Laughs Last.

Reasons Why Our Bob-Tailed Rooster is Not Doing His Duty,

And a Mellifuous Smile no More O'erspreads Our Countenance.

[Associated Press Telegrams.]

Albany Journal Gives up.

ALBANY, N. Y., Nov. 7.—The evening Journal, republican, concedes the election of Cleveland. There seems no longer any douot that Cleveland has been elected president.

Let us Weep.

NEW YORK, Nov. 7.—Cleveland now has a plurality of about 1,000 in this state. The vote will not be 200 on either side of these figures.

More Tears.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., Nov. 7.—Reports coming in slowly, and the result still in doubt. Both parties claim the state, the chances seeming to be in favor of Cleveland.

A Discourager.

MADISON, Wis., Nov. 7.—Returns not all in for Wisconsin, but there have been large democratic gains, perhaps enough to carry the state for Cleveland.

The Latest.

NEW YORK, Nov. 7.—Latest reports and estimate of four counties not heard faom give Clevelane the state by a plurality of 831.

Dakota to the Front.

BISMARCK, Nov. 7.—Returns from all over Dakota indicate a clean-up for the republican party. Montana is also republican, judging from the meager returns.
articles.summary: Associated Press telegrams dated Nov. 7 report Cleveland's apparent election as president (New York, Indiana, Wisconsin), while Dakota and Montana returns favor the Republicans; the Republican-leaning Cow Boy headlines its disappointment.

articles.headline: The Medora Stage & Forwarding Co.
articles.text: Since our last report, a large amount of work has been done on and for the line. The work on the route consists of improving the stations, fencing hay stacks, plowing fire guards around stations, digging wells and improving the road-bed. An additional station is being built between South Moreau and Indian Creek, dividing the long drive of twenty-two miles in half. In the way of passengers and express, many merchants have decided to ship everything via Medora, enough, in fact, to almost guarantee expenses. The road is well advertised in the Hills, and all outgoing passengers are anxious to try the new route. The matter of getting a mail contract is only a question of time, but even without this, and contrary to all expectation the road is now paying expenses. Arrangements have been made with all roads so that through tickets are being sold in Deadwood to all points in the world. The proprietors of the line have in all things consulted the comfort of passengers and have now the best coaches, the best stage stock, the best and shortest road-bed and the best system of connecting railroads of any stage line running into the Hills.
articles.summary: Report on improvements to the Medora–Black Hills stage line: station work, fire guards, wells, a new station between South Moreau and Indian Creek, through tickets sold in Deadwood, and the line paying expenses.

articles.text: Charles Stevenson, of Pittsburg, has been here for some time visiting his friends, the Eatons. He came to recuperate, but finds it rather expensive as he had to invest in several suits of more voluminous clothes.
articles.summary: Charles Stevenson of Pittsburg visiting the Eatons to recuperate.

articles.text: The coach coming in last evening from Deadwood made the best time that has ever been made by a stage on any line to or from the Hills. The time was thirty-four hours and thirty minutes. No endeavor was made toward fast time, and it is now proven beyond a doubt that thirty hours and less can easily be made. Tally another for Medora.
articles.summary: Deadwood coach arrived in record time of 34 hours 30 minutes.

articles.text: Medora presents quite an animated appearance at present. Buildings are going up on all sides, and if the weather continues as favorable as now, we will have several new buildings this year. Mr. J. C. Fisher is erecting two stores on Third avenue, near Main street, and when finished will add materially to the looks of that part of the town. The lumber for the new buildings of the N. P. R. C. Co. is arriving daily, and it will not be long before the company will have everything in readiness to supply the demands from their customers.
articles.summary: Building boom in Medora: J. C. Fisher erecting two stores on Third avenue; lumber arriving for N. P. R. C. Co. buildings.

articles.text: "The great grazing country of the west" is a section whose area is scarcply appreciated by most readers. It may be said to embrace a district 2,400 miles in length from north to south by about 1,000 miles from east to west.
articles.summary: The western grazing country is about 2,400 by 1,000 miles.

articles.text: The Northwestern Cattle Raisers association, of Texas, now offers $500 for the conviction of cattle thieves. Such sums as this will prove a great help in bringing the thieves and brand burners to their just deserts.—Ex.
articles.summary: Texas cattle raisers offer $500 for convicting cattle thieves (exchange).

articles.text: A private note to this office from Fort Maginnis, reports the steer crop rather short, on account of the depredations of thieves, half-breed Indians and wild animals, but says the stock at hand are of excellent quality.—[Miles City S. G. Journal.
articles.summary: Fort Maginnis steer crop short from thieves and wild animals (Miles City journal).

articles.text: The market is not overstocked with wool yet, despite all that may be said to that effect, as we paid over $40,000,000 for foreign wool last year. There is a demand for wool, and as long as we do not produce enough for our own use sheep-raising will result in profit.—Western Rural.
articles.summary: Wool market not overstocked (Western Rural).

articles.text: For the week ending with Saturday last fifty-two diseased hogs, nine cattle, nineteen quarters of beef, and five sheep, amounting in all to 15,000 lbs., were condemned. It takes constant and careful watching in and around the Chicago Stock Yards to prevent certain unscrupulous dealers from putting the meat of diseased animals on the market.
articles.summary: Diseased animals condemned at the Chicago Stock Yards.

articles.text: An old farmer tells us that there is no feed so good to keep animals in flesh during winter as scalded oats. For mares, cows and sheep that are to raise young ones it is superior to almost any other feed, as it not only puts the animal in good condition to furnish milk abundantly, but the young at birth are strong and active. Wheat bran is also an excellent feed for breeding animals given in the form of a mess.—[Western Rural.
articles.summary: Scalded oats recommended as winter feed (Western Rural).

articles.text: Northern Pacific cattle shipments this year have been the greatest since the road opened. The revenue from east-bound shipments already equals the earnings made last spring from west-bound shipments. So far, 50,000 head of beef cattle have been shipped east, and contracts already made call for the shipment of 25,000 more. Last spring 100,000 one and two-year-old cattle were shipped east.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific cattle shipments the greatest since the road opened: 50,000 beef cattle shipped east so far.

articles.text: Thursday a secret service detective from Montana arrived from up the river with Jack Wilson, better known as Club Foot Jack, in charge. Jack was wanted here for stealing a team of ponies from Long Wood about six weeks ago, and also for breaking into several shacks and stealing their contents. The prisoner was brought before Justice Stanton to-day and committed for trial at the next term of the district court. He takes a philosophic view of the situation and expects to "go over the road."—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Club Foot Jack Wilson brought to Mandan and committed for trial for horse theft (Mandan Pioneer).

articles.text: Some Tennessee breeders of throughbred horses have arranged a race for yearlings to be run at Gallatin during the middle of November, the distance being a quarter of a mile. Several years ago an attempt was made in England to institute a race for yearlings, but the Jockey Club promptly took the matter in hand and forbade anything of the kind being done. As a matter of fact there is little doubt that both English and American thoroughbreds have deteriorated considerably in point of stamina by reason of so many races at short distances, and for two and three-year-olds, being run.
articles.summary: Tennessee yearling race planned at Gallatin.

articles.text: A lot of horse stock was recently shipped from San Antonio, Texas, to Alaska.
articles.summary: Horses shipped from San Antonio to Alaska.

articles.summary: Leona pasture in Texas sold at $3 an acre.

articles.text: The United States is the greatest sheep raising country in the world, except Australia.
articles.summary: U.S. second only to Australia in sheep raising.

articles.text: Mr. John Splan, who drove Johnson during this season says that the pacer will make a mile in 2:02 some day.
articles.summary: John Splan predicts a 2:02 mile for the pacer Johnson.

articles.text: Five hundred dogs, valued at $500,000 are now on exhibition in a New York garden. Among them are the Esquimaux dogs brought by the Greeley relief expedition.
articles.summary: Dog show in New York includes Greeley expedition dogs.

articles.text: Why should there be thought any more indelicacy in using the name of a male than in speaking of a female animal? What possible objection is there to the words stallion, bull, ram, boar? We say man, woman, boy, girl, without a thought of need of any evasion of the question of sex. Yet many, especially in the presence of ladies, seen to think it indelicate to call our domestic animals by their correct name. In this connection it may be said that buck is not properly applied to a male sheep. Ram is the proper word in such case.—[Breeders' Gazette.
articles.summary: Plea to call male animals by their proper names (Breeders' Gazette).

articles.text: We do not understand why Governor Glick, of Kansas, should have quarantined against Iowa cattle. There has never been a case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia discovered in that State, and her laws are quite as well adapted to her protection as are those of Illinois, and they are faithfully and efficiently executed. When we first saw Governor Glick's proclamation, as transmitted by telegraph, we supposed the mention of Iowa to have been an error. We are informed, however, that it was correct, but are utterly at a loss to know why it should be so.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Questioning Kansas Governor Glick's quarantine of Iowa cattle (Breeder's Gazette).

articles.text: The attitude of the Northwest towards Texas cattle interests has been severely criticised by this and other papers, and the action of the representatives of the cattle interests of the Northwestern states and territories, in the St. Louis convention, will probably go to show whether or not those criticism are just. If they show a disposition to aid us in securing a national trail we shall feel that their quarantine may have been, after all, against Texas fever instead of against Texas cattle, and we shall straightway do them the justice to take back some of the unkind things we have said about them.—[San Antonio Stockman.
articles.summary: Texas view of Northwestern quarantine and the national trail (San Antonio Stockman).

articles.text: The Rev. John Biggs, a Baptist preacher from Sadorus, Ill., who stole several horses, a buggy, and $130 in money a few weeks ago, has just been sentenced by Judge Wilkin in the Douglas county circuit court to sixteen years in the penitentiary. Biggs had formerly been a hard character and had served a term in the penitentiary for horse stealing, but he kept his record from the people there, and, obtained a license from the Baptists to preach a year or more ago. Most of the stolen property was found in his possession when he was captured at Flora, Ill., and he was almost killed by jumping from the cars while being brought to Tuscola by Sheriff Wyatt.—Breeders' Gazette.
articles.summary: Baptist preacher John Biggs sentenced for horse theft in Illinois (Breeders' Gazette).

articles.text: Most persons feed their horses oats by measure, instead of weight, forgetting there is quite a difference in the weight of oats when different lots are measured. Some lots of oats are very heavy, and some quite light. Horses that are fed twelve quarts per day of heavy oats will fall off when changed to twelve quarts of light oats—there being from five to ten cent. loss of nutritious matter in them. It is always best to feed the best oats and hay to horses, but judgment is needed to regulate the quantity so as not to feed too much or too little. Many owners of horses trust the feeding entirely to their farm hands, who have little judgment and no care for the results. Owners of horses should determine the quantity required for their horses, and give strict instructions to have just the required amount fed. In this way horses can be kept in proper condition.—[Miles City S. G. Journal.
articles.summary: Feeding oats by weight rather than measure (Miles City journal).

articles.text: John Splan's dictum, that continual trial of horses from which a great performance is expected are in nearly every instance injurious, seems to be founded on fact. During the past week there were several trials against time by the best of our trotters, and in no instance were they successful. Maud S. started over the fast track at Hartford to beat her record of 2:09¾, made at Cleveland early in the season when her vitality had not been severely tried by continued training and when an absolute rest of a year had put her in good spirits and fettle to do her best. The Hartford trial was made only after weeks of careful preparation, and yet the best mile she could show was 2:12½, and after this exhibition Bair gave up the job in disgust. She has been hammered away at ever since last June, and evidently does not feel like making a great effort. At Lexington Elvira tried to beat her record of 2:18½, made at Cleveland a few weeks ago, and failed, 2:20 being her best mile. Nutbreaker, the fastest yearling ever bred east of the Rocky Mountains, was started to lower his mark of 2:43, and he failed. Splan is right. Once a year is often enough to give a very fast horse the best mile that can be got out of him. Continual trying only results in failure and disappointment.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Trotting trials against time fail; Splan's view upheld (Breeder's Gazette).

articles.text: "What's your's?" "Whisky." "Have some water?" "No, thanks; there's enough water in your whisky now."

articles.summary: Frank Gilman of Mandan passed through, bound for Helena car department.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens will be here in a few days as a permanent resident of Medora. The doctor is a live business man, with many years experience in the west, and will make a valuable citizen.
articles.summary: Dr. H. M. Jorgens to settle in Medora.

articles.text: Bob Roberts has been busily engaged in the construction of a beef corral for the N. P. R. C. Co. It will be 1,000 feet in circumference, and is situated about six miles north of here.

articles.text: Mr. Ellison, ice agent for the N. P. R. C. Co., is building a dam across the Little Missouri for the purpose of securing ice for the company. He intends to put up 25,000 tons at the different ice houses this season.
articles.summary: Ice agent Ellison damming the Little Missouri to put up 25,000 tons of ice.

articles.text: The other day our newsboy sold an elderly gentleman a copy of the Cow Boy. When he opened the paper and saw the brand advertisements, he exclaimed: "Oh, what pretty cows; but they are all the same breed."
articles.summary: Newsboy anecdote about the brand advertisements.

articles.text: "Go away from home to learn the news." A Medora gentlemen while in Mandan heard that three men had been caught, supposed to have set fire to Hotel de Mores, and that one of them had been found guilty and hanged. We have heard nothing about a hanging bee.
articles.summary: False Mandan rumor that men were hanged for setting fire to Hotel de Mores.

articles.text: Charles Cook, of Milbank, arrived last week, and will be a permanent resident of Medora. He is an energetic rustler and has come to stay. Mr. Cook will open a confectionery and tobacco store and dish up oysters in the highest style of the art. We welcome him and his family to Medora.
articles.summary: Charles Cook of Milbank arrives to open a confectionery, tobacco and oyster store.

articles.text: Considerable work is being done in the Medora coal mine preparatory to the winter trade. The tunnel is in about ninety feet, and a chamber fourteen feet square has been taken out. The coal is steadily improving in quality, and is now undoubtedly the best lignite that has been found in the west.
articles.summary: Work on the Medora coal mine: 90-foot tunnel, improving lignite.

articles.text: By mutual consent the firm of Boyd & Alexander, of the Pyramid Park Hotel, Little Missouri, dissolved partnership on the 1st of November, Mr. Boyd continuing the business, paying and collecting all bills. He will keep up the reputation of the hotel, and will spare no pains to make everything agreeable to those who are under his care. We wish him success.
articles.summary: Boyd & Alexander of the Pyramid Park Hotel dissolve partnership Nov. 1; Boyd continues.

articles.text: The Catholic church erected by the Marquise de Mores was blessed by Father Martin on Sunday last. A large congregation gathered to participate in the ceremonies, which were very impressive. Father Martin took his text from the temple of Solomon, and delivered an eloquent and instructive sermon. He urged that the Catholic people use every means to maintain the church in a manner creditable to a christian community, and that a school be established for the enlightenment of our young people. It is expected that the bishop will be here to dedicate the church early next spring. Father Martin intends to hold services in Medora at least once a month, and if he succeeds in procuring an assistant priest in Mandan, will be able to give us more frequent visits. Now that we have a place of worship, the community at large should not fail to appreciate the efforts of the Marquise in erecting the holy edifice.
articles.summary: Catholic church built by the Marquise de Mores blessed by Father Martin.

articles.text: Bob Roberts' bear creates no little amusement for the boys. She is as active and nimble as a cat, and never seems to tire in her funny capers. The other day some one gave bruin a bottle of beer, which seemed to please her very much. It made her tipsy, and her efforts to draw beer from the bottle were very ludicrous. She finally stood on her head and held the bottle between her paws and sucked it dry. It got the best of her, and she was compelled to lie down and sober up.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts' pet bear gets drunk on beer.
